#1465. Newcastle scrape past Millwall to extend Jaissle’s unbeaten start

Joe Willock’s deft finish ensured Newcastle United survived a tough test against Millwall to keep their excellent run in the Carabao Cup intact.

This competition had been fruitful for Newcastle under former manager Eddie Howe and although this match was hard work – as well as hard to watch at times – his successor Matthias Jaissle guided them through a difficult trip to south-east London.

He called it “job done,” and that was pretty much all it was. “We needed patience on one hand, but also to be passionate and tough. We had the chance [to score] and took it,” he said.

Newcastle have reached the semi-finals of this competition three times in the last four years, but struggled to get any sort of tempo going against their Championship opponents.

You could argue the winning goal came against the run of play late in the second half, moments after Millwall substitute Taïryk Arconte had smashed a low shot against the post.

"Livramento had a NIGHTMARE, he's so lucky" 😨Millwall were INCHES away from taking the lead against Newcastle 🤏 pic.twitter.com/X26aiTL432

Given they were missing 13 players because of injury, this was a brave display from Alex Neil’s side. They frustrated Newcastle for more than an hour, nullifying their attack, to the point where Jaissle’s team looked as though they had run out of ideas.

That was until Lewis Hall combined with Matias Fernandez-Pardo down the left and his drilled cross found Willock who cleverly used the angle to pass the ball into the net. Willock has been rejuvenated under Jaissle. He looked certain to be sold this summer but is now starting regularly under a new manager in the number 10 role his system demands. It has been a nice redemption arc for the former Arsenal academy graduate.

Moments after Millwall hit the post, Joe Willock strikes to put Newcastle in front! ⚽️ pic.twitter.com/rSB8yV6NRO

The victory is all that matters and extends Jaissle’s unbeaten start to five games. Given he arrived just three weeks before the start of the season, that deserves praise even if it is obvious there is a lot of work to be done to improve their offensive play.

Playing in their lilac, or should that be Parma-violet, third kit for the first time, Newcastle looked off colour in the first half. Even though Jaissle named a strong team packed with experience of English cup ties, they struggled to overpower Millwall.

There were a few half-chances as Willock forced a save and Jacob Murphy fired over. There was a header missed from a corner by Sven Botman, which should have hit the target and Yoane Wissa also mistimed his jump after finding space for another header.

Millwall’s two centre-backs, Jake Cooper and Caleb Taylor were immense, flinging themselves in the way of every shot and clearing every loose ball that came into their vicinity. Given their injuries, this was a performance full of fight and defiance from the home side.

However, there was also an absence of quality in the final third from Newcastle, the same lack of cohesion and incision that was apparent at home to Bournemouth last weekend and in the first half away at Tottenham Hotspur.

It meant Millwall were happy to play for set-pieces close to the Newcastle box and Taylor got in front of his marker, flashing a header wide of the post.

That lacklustre first half meant Jaissle’s side had mustered just five shots on target in five halves of football since the 3-2 win over West Bromwich Albion in the previous round of the Carabao Cup.

Millwall started the second period like a side sensing Newcastle were vulnerable. A thunderbolt from Jenson Metcalfe, after the visitors had struggled to clear two crosses, almost gave them a spectacular lead.

Newcastle saw lots of the ball. Millwall were happy enough to let them have it given how little they were hurting them.

So much of Newcastle’s play was slow and cumbersome. Their set-piece delivery was also largely inept.

Neil’s side retained a threat and came so close to taking the lead when, not for the first time, a long ball forward caught the Newcastle defence out of shape and Tino Livramento’s mistake allowed Arconte to run clear and hit the post from a tight angle.

Well in, @Joewillock! 💪 pic.twitter.com/5a8G7lzD3H

Speaking after the game, Millwall manager Alex Neil said: “I’m very proud, I don’t think we deserved to lose that game.

“We had some good moments, and we got done by a bit of sucker punch at the end. But I’m very proud of the lads.”

As for their injury problems, he added: “I didn’t bring the teenagers on as a token gesture, I need to keep the first-team players fit. We’re really at bare bones.

But we beat Bolton at the weekend, got a couple of defeats before that but we started the season really well and once we get everybody back, we’ll be in good shape.”

With the first of the 16 teams through tonight, the draw won’t take place until most of the teams have played next week.

The draw will be shown on Sky Sports on Wednesday 16th Sept, after Manchester United play Brighton. Man City vs Norwich will be the only game outstanding then.

The third round had to be spread over two weeks as the nine Premier League sides in UEFA competitions entered the tournament in this round, as the same time as their Champions League and Europa League fixtures began. To avoid clubs facing clashes, the EFL split the fixtures across the two gameweeks.

Still got some more post-match to come for you, but we’ve got scores from all our matches tonight now:

From the Champions League, Man City held out against Porto to win 2-0.

“I think we had a lot of chances in the first half, and we went in a half-time saying we need to  take our chances, so I’m glad we came out in the second half and we did,” said Willock after the match.

“100% [the competition is important], we’ve won it before so it’s very important to us, but every game is important to us. Especially with a new coach and a lot of new players, we wanted to start the new season well. I think we started really well and we need to continue and this was a big game in keeping that momentum.”

"We said at half-time we NEED to take our chances"Lewis Hall and Joe Willock react to Newcastle's win over Millwall 🎙️ pic.twitter.com/NDF3laD8nT

Take a look at the match-winner from Joe Willock:

Moments after Millwall hit the post, Joe Willock strikes to put Newcastle in front! ⚽️ pic.twitter.com/rSB8yV6NRO

The goal came minutes after Millwall were inches away from taking the lead themselves, as Arconte was denied by the post:

"Livramento had a NIGHTMARE, he's so lucky" 😨Millwall were INCHES away from taking the lead against Newcastle 🤏 pic.twitter.com/X26aiTL432

We’ll be bringing you more from the post-match now.

Joe Willock has done enough for Newcastle to reach the fourth round and keep the travelling fans singing all the way back to the North-East.

It won’t go down in history as the greatest Carabao fixture, but Newcastle found a way to keep their momentum going and give Matthias Jaissle a win on his cup debut.

Newcastle aren’t taking any risks as Hornicek sends the ball long, and the players keep looking to send the ball down-field.

Seconds to go now. Marschall sends it long for one last effort, but it is cleared out of the box...

Willock has come off now for Newcastle’s own teenager, Sean Steur. A few more minutes and the man now on the bench with have done enough to send his side through to the next round.

We’re into the final minutes as Millwall are throwing everything at this.

Millwall are not out of this yet, as Neghli comes down the left side, twisting his way into the box past his defender – but having done the hard work, his shot flashes low across goal.

Some more changes, as Ramsey comes off for Newcastle, replaced by Lewis Miley.

A double change for the hosts as Dykes and Kelly come off for Regan Monty and Alfie Massey – the former just 15 years old.

Seconds later, another teenager takes to the pitch for Millwall as Osei-Tutu is replaced by 17-year-old Tristan Parkes.

Newcastle almost have another! From the sublime to the ridiculous, as Willock makes another run, this time down the left, and passes the ball onto the edge of the box where Elanga meets it in space. He lets it run, before taking his shot, but it is straight to Marschall.

Finally Newcastle have their breakthrough! They punish Millwall as Fernandez-Pardo feeds Hall on the left, who cuts inside and slips the ball across goal, finding Willock to redirect the ball to slot it home.

Marschall releases Arconte with a long ball and he turns Livramento to find huge amounts of space on the right side. He races into the box and takes a shot from close range, aiming for his near post, but is denied by the woodwork and the rebound hits the seated Hornicek. The keeper is lucky to not concede an own goal, as the ball bounces up and over his leg.

Issoufou again racing down the right side, before cutting inside and taking a shot with his left foot. Hall, who has been so crucial in the Newcastle attack, throws himself at the shot, and it flies high for Hornicek to collect.

Replays show that González, who Millwall players claimed had handled the ball earlier, leant down to clear with his shoulder.

Issoufou sends a great ball in for Millwall from the right side, but it is cleared by a Newcastle player, accompanied by cries for handball.

The game is opening up now as Newcastle make a run of their own, with Willock creating an opening for Elanga to take the ball to the edge of the box, before Taylor slides in to block his shot.

Millwall could absolutely win this with a smash-and-grab with less than 20 minutes to go. They are pushing for it but are lacking some attacking quality to finish the job.

From six shots they’ve had two on target, compared to Newcastle’s three on target from 20.

Fernandez-Pardo gets his first look at the ball, making a very quick run down across the centre of the field to the left side, but Osei-Tutu stays with him and takes him all the way to the back line before giving up a corner.

Elanga takes the corner, punched away by the keeper but no one goes to finish the job and Newcastle get another corner.

Metcalfe, who had his red card overturned this week, is the first player to go in the book for a mistimed challenge on Ramsey.

Just a reminder that there is no extra time, so if we’re all square after 90 minutes, it’s straight to a penalty shoot-out.

Willock gets the ball on the edge of the area and passes it on a quick turn to Barnes just inside the box, but there was not much on his shot and Marschall collects easily.

Double change now for Newcastle as Wissa and Murphy come off, replaced by Elanga and Fernandez-Pardo as Jaissle looks for pace. Schar is handed the armband.

Free kick for Newcastle, right on the corner of the box. Murphy takes, but it hits the wall 10 feet away, and bounces straight back to him. His cross into the box is headed out, and for all the opportunities Newcastle have created, they are yet to find the breakthrough.

We’ve also had a double change for Millwall as Esse and Lovelace have come off, replaced by Issoufou and Arconte.

What colour would you describe this Newcastle away shirt? They look like the sweets Purple Violet to me. Although would you call it an all Lilac number?

It’s the first time they have worn their third kit. Not sure whether I like it or not.  Shame The Den isn’t a sell out although I’m told tickets were priced at £31 and Millwall have a lot of injuries too.

Newcastle get another corner after a run from Willock. The delivery from Hall creates a good amount of confusion in the box and Marschall isn’t sure whether to stay on his line or come out to punch it away. From within the bodies, Wissa tries to get a shot off from close range but it bounces and the keeper easily collects.

González commits another foul, pulling down Esse, to give Millwall another free kick from 40 yards out.

The ball meets Taylor at the back post, but he meets it in the air and can’t quite direct it either into goal or back into the six-yard box, so it goes out for a Newcastle goal kick.

Another half chance for Millwall as Dykes feeds Kelly on the right side, who runs into the box and gets caught between passing the ball in and taking the shot, with the ball going high over the box.

Another great challenge from Osei-Tutu as Willock makes a run into the box, but is brought down by a well-timed tackle from the right-back.

The corner from Hall is better, but headed out and cleared.

Barnes again with space on the left side and he sends a ball fizzing low across the box to the far post but Neghli is able to lean on Murphy to stop him making contact.

Scramble for Newcastle as the ball is sent by Dykes to Neghli free at the far post, who puts the ball into a very dangerous area just in front of goal and everyone jumps on. Newcastle get to it first, managing to clear it from the goal mouth. It is cleared outside the box and it bounces to unmarked Metcalfe, who takes a thunderous shot, putting his laces through the ball but he is unable to keep it down and it goes over the bar.

Despite Alex Neil’s premonitions, no changes for Millwall at the break.

Right-back change for Newcastle, as Dedic comes off and Tino Livramento comes on.

The earlier kick-offs of the Carabao third round have just started their second periods, but here are the latest scores:

Aston Villa won their opening Champions League fixture 3-2 against Club Brugge, while Man City are still goalless against Porto, which you can follow with our live blog here

And that’s the last action of the half, as just one minute was added on and that was taken up by Newcastle’s corner.

Nothing separates the two sides at the half, thought the visitors have dominated in terms of possession and chances.

Millwall have held fast and will be happy to be finishing the half level. We may see some changes from them after the break.

The game is opening up before half-time, and Newcastle go again with Hall and Barnes. Osei-Tutu does well to wait before going in to block Barnes’s shot and send the ball behind for another Newcastle corner.

The delivery is once again poor, but Schar is pulled down inside the box by Taylor and is furious that nothing was given. There’s no VAR so there’s no review to consider – but looking at replays, Millwall were very lucky to get away with that foul.

Cooper makes a perfect pass down the left sideline, allowing Neghli to find space and forcing Newcastle to clear it away fo a Millwall corner.

The ball in is promising but Hornicek gets to it and punches it away, but the hosts keep the pressure on.

Baggott floats another ball across the box towards the right back post, but Hornicek easily collects the ball as Neghli can’t quite connect.

Newcastle moving the ball well again across midfield and it comes to Schar, who runs into space and gets a low shot away, around 40 yards out. It  takes a slight deflection on its way, going just wide of the post.

González is not having his best night and makes a silly foul against Dykes on the sideline, giving the hosts another set piece. The swinging ball in is not nearly as good as last time, and only reaches the first man, Newcastle’s Ramsey.

Millwall get a free kick, and the delivery is good, allowing Taylor to connect on the header inside the box. He beats Hornicek but the header rolls just wide of the post, to the groans of the home fans.

Hall goes short with the corner and Dedic has lots of time to cross the ball in from the right. It’s headed away but Millwall can’t break on the counter.

That sums up the game pretty well: not much finishing quality from Newcastle but Millwall not creating much from their limited spells of possession.

Newcastle pushing again. Another ball pulled back by Barnes finds Ramsey at the top of the box, and his ball in connects with Wissa. Newcastle’s captain can’t head it in the right direction though and Millwall survive again.

The spell of pressure results in another corner for the visitors – and now we’re getting some pushing in the six-yard box.

I think Millwall have done well. They have limited Newcastle to half chances and the odd set piece threat. They have made things really difficult for the visitors, crowding them out of space on the edge of the area.

When the home side have advanced up the pitch the Newcastle defence has not looked particularly secure.

As we reach the half-hour mark, Newcastle have 10 shots to Millwall’s one, though they sit one apiece on shots on target.

Esse gets caught on his heels as Hall pulls a long ball back on the left, and in the crowd at the top of the box Willock takes a shot, pulling it wide – cheers from the home crowd again.

First piece of good attacking play from Millwall as Neghli and Baggott work on the overlap. Baggott lofts a high ball to the back post, where Dykes gets a foot on it on the volley, but he can’t quite get over it and it’s easily picked up by Hornicek.

Barnes and Ramsey combine again down the left, with the midfielder trying to feed Barnes on his run. The pass has too much on it though, and as it runs out the back it’s met with jeers from the home fans for a goal kick.

Wissa breaks away down the centre of the field, with Barnes on his left, using him as a decoy. Wissa takes the shot though and it is blocked by a sliding defender.

Newcastle hit 20 minutes in with 68 per cent possession but nothing to show yet for their efforts. You feel like it will only be a matter of time though.

Another Newcastle corner, swung in well and Botman comes charging in, beating cooper to a free header. The defender heads it over the bar and holds his head in his hands. The visitors could definitely be a goal up by now.

Hall’s free-kick is met by the first man Metcalfe who heads it away to atone for his foul and Newcastle remain stymied.

Millwall will have expected Newcastle to dominate the ball but they are really pushing for an opener, especially down the left side with Barnes and Hall.

Again, Newcastle coming down the wings, this time on the left. Esse picks the ball up but loses it and Willock picks it up and takes a shot on his right foot with good power but sends it straight at Marschall. The debut keeper parries it away and it’s cleared by a  Millwall header.

Willock comes down the left soon after and is fouled by Metcalfe to get a free kick in a good spot outside the box.

Murphy gets a shot off after Dedic picks up a long ball on the right side and crosses it back towards the middle of the field. Murphy gets on it and takes the shot inside the box off his left foot but it sails over the bar.

González gives the ball away cheaply and Metcalfe picks it up, but unable to move it forward.

Newcastle will need to make sure they don’t get complacent in defence.

Millwall having a spell of possession, the counter-attack looking like their best option but as they move down the right hand side, Lovelace makes a late challenge to get the ball back and fouls Wissa.

Newcastle advancing, with Dedic and Ramsey moving the ball across midfield. Barnes gets the ball on the left of the box, and his ball is in knocked out and Newcastle get the first corner of the game.

Nothing comes of it as it is sent in high and long over the box.

Fair to say both teams are settling, but Millwall try and create a chance with Lovelace, though it’s intercepted. Dykes takes a bit of a knock and is slow to get up.

Here we go in south London, and Millwall get us started.

Just a reminder of the teams starting today:

Starting XI: Filip Marschall; Jordi Osei-Tutu, Caleb Taylor, Jake Cooper, Elkan Baggott; Lyndon Dykes, Jenson Metcalfe; Camiel Neghli, Daniel Kelly, Romain Esse; Zak Lovelace

Substitutes: Regan Monty, Tristan Parkes, Sacha Vieira, George Beaumont, Yanis Issoufou, George Evans, Taïryk Arconte, Alfie Massey, Zak Sturge

Starting XI: Lukás Hornícek; Lewis Hall, Fabian Schär, Amar Dedic, Sven Botman; Jacob Murphy, Nico González; Jacob Ramsey, Harvey Barnes, Joe Willock; Yoane Wissa

Substitutes: Tino Livramento, Anthony Elanga, Malick Thiaw, Nick Pope, Lewis Miley, Bazoumana Touré, Matias Fernandez-Pardo, Aladji Bamba, Sean Steur

The teams are coming out of the tunnel, and both home and away fans in the Den are already in loud voice. Kick off on the way!

"We've tried to find the right balance" ⚖️Matthias Jaissle on his team selection for tonight's match with Millwall ⚫️ pic.twitter.com/kiRRxAgLk8

We’re just a few minutes away from kick off in south London, but Bournemouth have scored the first goal of the third round, with Ryan Christie putting his side ahead against Lincoln.

Alex Neil has not minced his words over his squad’s injury crisis. His team is down 13 players, which the coach says has “definitely forced” his hand in terms of squad rotation.

Playing two matches a week in the “relentless” Championship has turned his squad selection into a “needs must scenario” and he even admitted he “may need to make a couple of changes at half-time depending on how the game goes”

Matthias Jaissle is clearly taking this competition seriously and having started the league well, he is still trying to get the fans onside and create momentum for his team.

At the same time, Telegraph Sport have reported that Ross Wilson, the sporting director, has warned there will have to be more departures in future windows. Having lost Alexander Isak, Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and Bruno Guimarães in 12 months, there will be yet be more upheaval.

You can read Luke Edwards’ full story on that here

The Premier League teams playing in European competitions enter the EFL Cup in this round, with all 16 fixtures being played over five match days. As well as tonight’s games there will be:

Fleetwood Town vs Sheffield United (7.45pm)

*all kick-off at 8pm, unless stated otherwise

Newcastle have named a strong side – probably the strongest they could field when factoring in senior players needing game time – to take on Millwall in the Carabao Cup.

Jacob Ramsey impressed coming off the bench against Bournemouth last weekend and manager Matthias Jaissle refused to sanction winger Jacob Murphy’s transfer to Nottingham Forest late in the window. Both deserve a chance to impress from the start.

Veteran centre back Fabian Schar comes in for Malick Thiaw, but those are the only three changes from the side that drew with Bournemouth.

Jaissle insisted he would take the competition seriously and the teamsheet proves it, but it also raises questions about some of Newcastle’s summer recruitment.

Bazoumana Toure cost £42m but was withdrawn at half time in the win over West Brom in the previous round, which means Harvey Barnes does not get a rest. That’s a lot of money to spend on a winger who has not looked Premier League ready so far.

Aladji Bamba, a £30m signing from Monaco, has not started a game yet and has been an unused substitute since the opening game against Liverpool. He remains on the bench.

Even Sean Steur, who has looked good since his summer move from Ajax, cannot dislodge another more recent arrival in former Manchester City midfielder Nico González.

Having made a total of eight new signings in a much-vaunted summer rebuild, Jaissle only started three of them against Bournemouth and only two start tonight at The Den.

Early days but this was one of the main reasons Eddie Howe quit – he did not think the likes of Toure, Steur and Bamba were ready to play first team football.

The visitors have arrived in south London

We've made it to South East London 👋 pic.twitter.com/nh8Fpa37xT

We’re bringing you the action from the pick of tonight’s EFL Cup games but there are also four games kicking off at 7.45pm:

The Champions League also returns tonight and you can follow along with both our blogs:

Aston Villa are currently 3-1 up against Club Brugge in Belgium – follow the action here

Manchester City will face Porto at 8.00pm – our live blog has just gone live here with the team news from both sides

Yoane Wissa takes the captain’s armband tonight, while Jacob Ramsey starts up front after scoring a late equaliser against Bournemouth on Saturday

Your Mags at Millwall ✊ pic.twitter.com/zfnHgTlWgh

Keeper Filip Marschall is making his debut while Jensen Metcalfe is back in the squad after his red card against Bolton was overturned on appeal

How your Lions line-up tonight 🔢 pic.twitter.com/wEp6qLIz4Y

Welcome to tonight’s live coverage of Millwall vs Newcastle United, as the Geordies travel to south London for the third round of the Carabao Cup.

Newcastle held off West Brom in their second-round match, with Harvey Barnes scoring two second-half goals to see his side through. It was a mighty comeback, after Isaac Price scored early to stun the crowd at St James’ Park. Bazoumana Toure equalised for Matthias Jaissle’s side just before half-time, and Barnes, his replacement in the second half, put them ahead minutes after the restart. West Brom pulled it back to 2-2 with a penalty converted by Price after Lewis Hall was deemed to have handled the ball in the box, but Barnes got his second just nine minutes from full-time and the hosts were able to see out the match to progress.

Alex Neil’s Millwall have reached round three via a 0-1 win over Cambridge United, following a penalty shoot-out in the first round to beat QPR. They come into this tie with a squad stretched thin, as they have been hit with an injury crisis a month into the new season. Millwall have confirmed that they will be without Casper De Norre, Josh Coburn, Tristan Crama, Alfie Doughty, Mathis Servais, Ryan Leonard, Mihailo Ivanovic, Lukas Jensen and Luke Cundle.

Both sides sit seventh in their respective leagues, with Millwall on a record of three wins and two losses this season, while Newcastle remain unbeaten (two draws and a win).

Newcastle will hoping to progress smoothly in a tournament that they have recently enjoyed good form in – winners in 2025 and semi-finalists last season – and with Millwall dealing with a bare bones squad, the Championship side are the underdogs on paper going into this fixture.

But, as always, anything can happen, so let us know your score prediction in the comments and we’ll be bringing you team news soon!

#1464. Fenerbahce 3-2 Liverpool: Sloppy Reds wilt in Turkey again as Dirk Kuyt masterminds famous Champions League win against his error-strewn old side

Published: 14:54 EDT, 4 November 2026 | Updated: 03:15 EDT, 5 November 2026

The mad metropolis of Istanbul was the setting for one of Liverpool’s greatest nights, when this storied old club won the 2005 Champions League final down the road at the Ataturk Stadium – but right now fans will be glad to see the back of Turkey for a while.

For the third time in just over 13 months, the English giants have travelled to the bustling hub on the banks of the Bosphorus only to wilt amid the deafening noise of a Turkish football stadium.

They lost twice to Galatasaray last season and now, over the river to the Asian side of the intercontinental Istanbul, Liverpool fell flat at the hands of Fenerbahce – thanks to two Englishmen and a friend-turned-foe in the dugout.

Mason Greenwood and Archie Brown, born in Bradford and Birmingham respectively, both scored for Fenerbahce before Vedat Muriqi scored a winner as caretaker manager Dirk Kuyt, once a cult hero at Anfield, recorded a win in his final game in the dugout.

He will soon be replaced by ex-Newcastle and 101-cap Turkey midfielder Emre Belozoglu but Kuyt will not be forgetting this evening in a hurry in front of a raucous, hostile crowd in the district of Kadikoy.

As for Liverpool, who jetted home straight after the game and were due to land around 2am English time, they and boss Andoni Iraola were just glad to get out of Turkey, probably with their ears still ringing.

It was a poor night for Liverpool as they went down 3-2 against Fenerbahce in Istanbul

Andoni Iraola's side let a second-half lead slip and there were some terrible errors

Archie Brown sunk to his knees in celebration at full-time as the home crowd erupted

Trey Nyoni had scored his first goal in professional football and then Alexander Isak headed home to put Liverpool 2-1 up two minutes after coming on as a substitute but they were undone by sloppy defensive errors.

That will give Iraola plenty to ponder in the coming weeks given his side have conceded nine goals in their last three European games, all to opposition that would not be counted as part of the continent’s best in LASK, Villarreal and now Fenerbahce.

Aside from a UEFA Super Cup triumph over Chelsea at the home of Besiktas in 2019, Liverpool have struggled in this country and their last Turkish delight came against Trabzonspor, who now employ a certain Mohamed Salah, back in 2010.

Fenerbahce and Kuyt celebrated a famous win – as did around 45,000 home fans who produced deafening whistles every time Liverpool had the ball.

It was a true attack on the senses and Iraola’s side felt it, with several passes going astray as Kuyt’s men had the best of the first-half action and were unlucky to go into the break level at 1-1.

Liverpool had gone ahead on 25 minutes through Nyoni’s first goal in professional football, when a header from English full back Brown fell straight into the path of the Reds midfielder, who charged on to the ball like he was Steven Gerrard.

He needed a deflection off defender Kojo Peprah Oppong but cared not a jot as his volley ended up beating former Manchester City man Ederson.

It continued a stellar season for 19-year-old Nyoni, who has had a fairytale week that included a first Premier League start, first professional goal and also talks over a bumper new contract. To say it would be deserved would be the understatement of the season.

Trey Nyoni opened the scoring for the Reds but his goal came in a losing effort

Alexander Isak headed Liverpool back in front after some terrible Fenerbahce defending

FENERBAHCE (4-3-3): Ederson 5; Semedo 5 (Muldur 75), Skriniar 6, Peprah 6, BROWN 8; Guendouzi 7, Kante 7, Yuksek 5; Greenwood 8 (Aydin 89), Lukaku 7 (Muriqi 63, 6), Kahveci 7 (Arturkoglu 75).

Subs not used: Cetin, Gunok, Efe Demir, Mercan, Elmaz, Nene, Mimovic.

Scorers: Greenwood 29, Brown 73, Muriqi 79.

LIVERPOOL (4-2-3-1): Alisson 4; Gomez 5 (Wirtz 66, 6), Jacquet 5, Van Dijk 4, Tsimikas 4 (Kerkez 76); Nyoni 8 (Koumas 85), Mac Allister 7; Munoz 5 (Isak 66, 6), Szoboszlai 5, Ngumoha 7 (Gakpo 67, 6); Barcola 5.

Subs not used: Mamardashvili, Woodman, Araujo, Chambers, McConnell, Danns.

Nyoni’s goal, in theory, should have helped Liverpool settle. As it was, it did anything but.

Fenerbahce came out roaring and hit the bar instantly through Irfan Can Kahveci. With the next attack, they were level, just four minutes after falling behind.

Just like Liverpool’s goal, the Turkish side needed a hefty deflection to help them. Greenwood took a free-kick from 25 yards, Jeremy Jacquet turned his back on it and foxed Alisson. Two Brazilian goalkeepers, two wicked deflections that neither could do anything about.

Alisson was the best away player on the pitch in that opening 45 minutes, thwarting Greenwood, the brute force of Romelu Lukaku and fellow former Premier League favourite N'Golo Kante, who is now 35 but still has the energy of the young whippersnapper we all knew and loved.

Iraola turned to his bench with a £285million triple-change and two of them combined just minutes later, Cody Gakpo crossing for Isak to head home his seventh of the season.

But just as when they went 1-0 ahead, Liverpool retreated and invited pressure. A Kante cross was not dealt with by Gakpo and Brown could ghost in at the back post to score.

Then, on 79 minutes, Muriqi thumped home a header to put Fenerbahce 3-2 up and on their way to a memorable night.

Liverpool, who would have taken a huge step towards qualification with a win here, still have work to do.

#1463. A spatiotemporal cancer cell trajectory underlies glioblastoma heterogeneity

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Cancer cells show highly heterogeneous and plastic states in glioblastoma, an incurable brain tumour1,2,3,4,5. However, how these malignant states arise and whether they follow defined cellular trajectories across tumours is poorly understood. Here we generated a deep single-cell and spatial multi-omic atlas of human glioblastoma that pairs transcriptomic, epigenomic and genomic profiling of 12 tumours across many regions. We identify that glioblastoma heterogeneity is driven by spatially patterned transitions of cancer cells from developmental-like states towards those defined by a glial injury response and hypoxia. This cellular trajectory regionalizes tumours into distinct tissue microenvironments and manifests in a molecularly conserved manner across tumours as well as genetically distinct tumour subclones. Consistently, using a new deep-learning framework to map cancer cell states jointly with clones in situ, we show that tumour subclones are finely spatially intermixed through glioblastoma tissue microenvironments. We validate this cellular trajectory by using somatic mutation-based hierarchies in vivo and an experimental patient-derived organoid model ex vivo. Finally, we show that this cancer cell trajectory is intimately linked to myeloid heterogeneity and unfolds across regionalized myeloid signalling environments. Our findings define a stereotyped trajectory of cancer cells in glioblastoma and unify glioblastoma tumour heterogeneity into a tractable cellular and tissue framework.

The extensive tumour heterogeneity of glioblastoma (GB), an incurable adult brain cancer, presents a major obstacle to treatment. Nearly two decades of molecular profiling has found that malignant cells exist across a spectrum of cellular states within each tumour, resembling developmental neural progenitors as well as mesenchymal-like and injury response states1,2,3,4,5. These states are suggested to vary in abundance across tumours and stratify GBs into subtypes1,2. Furthermore, patient-derived xenografts have shown that malignant cells can transition across cellular states, indicating their plasticity2,6. Despite these extensive efforts, we still do not understand how cancer cells diversify into distinct states and give rise to GB heterogeneity. In particular, whether malignant cells follow stereotyped or variable cellular trajectories across GB tumours is unknown. A cancer cell trajectory that is conserved and tractable across GBs would present a highly attractive therapeutic target.

Single-cell, bulk and spatial genomics have revealed stereotypical aspects of GBs. Several malignant cell states can be detected within each tumour2,5,7 and their single-cell transcriptional profiles can be mapped onto an axis between developmental-like (dev-like) and injury response-associated gene expression programs4,8. Genetic heterogeneity1,2 and tumour microenvironment (TME) signals9 also influence malignant cell state identity. Furthermore, these states show a recurrent spatial organization across tumours5,10. Yet, these observations have not been linked together to resolve malignant cellular trajectories in GB, in part due to the lack of multimodal profiling efforts that can integrate insights from various cell and tissue atlassing technologies. Here we address this challenge by means of deep single-cell and spatial multi-omic profiling of human GBs and identify that a stereotyped spatiotemporal trajectory of cancer cells gives rise to GB heterogeneity.

To comprehensively profile GB heterogeneity, we generated a single-cell and spatial multi-omic atlas of 12 isocitrate dehydrogenase wild-type (IDH-wt) primary GB tumours (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Table 1), combining three main approaches. First, we profiled each tumour across many sites, ranging from 4 sites (roughly 1.25 cm3 each) for most cases to 15 sites effectively covering one whole tumour (Extended Data Fig. 1a and Supplementary Fig. 1), spanning 57 tumour sites in total. Second, we generated paired single-nuclei and spatial omic data from each sampling site, profiling consecutive tissue sections with single-nuclei joint transcriptome sequencing and chromatin accessibility sequencing (‘multiome’ snRNA + ATAC-seq) and Visium spatial transcriptomics (ST) (Fig. 1a). Select sites were assayed with orthogonal Xenium ST and immunohistochemistry, as well as whole-genome sequencing (WGS) of tumour microbiopsies (Supplementary Fig. 1). Third, we profiled large numbers of nuclei (more than 1 million) and spatial tissue sections (more than 0.3 million spatial transcriptomes across 97 Visium sections) (Supplementary Table 2). The resulting ‘GBM-space’ dataset, accessible on a user-friendly interactive webportal11 (www.gbmspace.org/), enables comprehensive multimodal characterization of GB and presents a unique holistic tumour atlas for cancer research.

a, Schematic illustration of the experimental design and primary aims of this study. b, Overview of the cellular composition of our GBM-space atlas. Uniform manifold approximation and projection visualization of the snRNA-seq profiles of malignant and TME cells outlining the main constituent populations, and a ring plot illustrating the relative distribution of cells at three levels of granularity: malignant (657,275 cells) versus TME (368,054 cells) status, coarse-level populations (text labels around the outer ring) and fine-grained cell states. c, Dendrogram depicting transcriptomic clustering of malignant cell states (top) and their biological characteristics, including their hierarchical annotation, distribution of expression signatures from ref. 2, distribution of cell states across patient tumours, marker gene expression and significantly enriched MSigDB pathways. Malignant clusters present across more than 50% of the tumours are shown in bold. d, Intra-tumour and inter-tumour GB cell state heterogeneity across our dataset. The bar plot (left) shows cell state distribution summarized across each tumour. The dot plot (right) depicts the top cell state for a given sampling site within a given tumour (colour) and its relative abundance (size). Ast., astrocyte; Exc., excitatory neurons; Inh., inhibitory neurons; Lymph., lymphocytes; OPC-n-like, OPC-neuron-like; Prolif., proliferative; Vasc. vasculature. Illustrations in a created in BioRender; Lee, J. https://biorender.com/5lvlyxp (2026).

To examine GB heterogeneity, we first annotated malignant and TME cell states in our multiome data. After standard data processing workflows, we filtered nuclei on the basis of quality of both RNA and ATAC profiles, resulting in 1,025,329 nuclei with more than 85,000 nuclei per tumour on average (Methods, Fig. 1a and Extended Data Fig. 1b,c). We then annotated transcriptomic cell states in snRNA-seq data and examined ATAC data in a companion study to map GB gene regulatory networks12.

We integrated snRNA-seq data using scVI13 to account for batch variations, then distinguished malignant clusters on the basis of inferred copy number (CN) gain of chromosome (chr.) 7 and loss of chr. 10, as well as enrichment of known GB expression programs2 (Fig. 1b and Supplementary Figs. 2 and 3). Subclustering yielded 28 malignant clusters, including 10 highly common clusters present across 50% of the tumours, as well as 71 TME clusters (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Fig. 4).

We annotated malignant clusters by relating them to GB cell state gene programs described in ref. 2 and developing human brain single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) data14 as well as gene-set enrichment analysis (Methods and Supplementary Fig. 5a,b). As a result, we hierarchically grouped malignant clusters into four main classes and nine subclasses of GB cell states that were each observed across several tumours (Fig. 1c,d, Supplementary Fig. 4a and Supplementary Table 4).

Two main classes of GB cell states resembled distinct developmental progenitors: neural progenitor-like and oligodendrocyte progenitor-like (NPC-OPC-like) and neuronal progenitor-like and neuronal-like (NPC-neuronal-like) cells. These two dev-like states matched those previously described in ref. 2 and expressed respective developmental markers of oligodendrocyte (PDGFRA, OLIG1) and neuronal lineages (MYT1L, STMN2) (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Note 1).

The third main GB cell state showed a transcriptomic spectrum from astrocyte progenitor (AC-prog)-like to gliosis-like (that is, glial injury response) and hypoxic states, broadly expressing core astrocyte markers (SLC1A3, GFAP) (Fig. 1c). Whereas AC-prog-like cells showed Neftel ‘AC-like’ signatures and resembled developmental glioblasts, AC-gliosis and gliosis-like cells expressed genes related to wound healing and injury response (VIM, SERPINE1) and angiogenesis (VEGFA) and the remaining cells were defined by hypoxia (HILPDA) (Fig. 1c). The gliosis-hypoxic cells were initially described as mesenchymal-like states1,2 defined by Neftel ‘MES1-2’ programs. Recently, they were reinterpreted as more similar to reactive astrocytes responding to injury4 and glial wound healing states4,8. Here we adopted the latter nomenclature that better reflected malignant cellular trajectories in our atlas (sections below). The final main malignant state represented proliferative cells. Although dominated by G2M and S phase gene expression, we resolved that these cells represent actively cycling analogues of main GB cell states (Fig. 1c, Supplementary Fig. 6a and Supplementary Note 1).

GB cell states showed substantial inter-tumour and intra-tumour heterogeneity. Most tumours showed a dominant GB cell state among the main classes (for example, NPC-OPC-like for AT5 and 9) (Fig. 1d, left). However, despite their stratification, each tumour contained substantial fractions of both dev-like and AC-gliosis-hypoxia cells. Two tumours (AT4 and 10) showed near equal proportions of both classes, whereas in others, the minority states represented 5–21% of all malignant cells (Fig. 1d and Supplementary Table 4). Individual sampling sites also contained a mixture of GB states broadly reflecting the parent tumour (Supplementary Fig. 8b,c). Yet, we could often identify at least one site per tumour with a unique cell state composition. In a striking example, tumour AT10 showed distinct dominant GB cell states at each site (Fig. 1d, right). Consistent with other studies5,7,15, these observations show that single biopsies can be confounded to stratify GB tumour phenotypes.

We also captured all main cell lineages in the GB TME (Supplementary Figs. 4b and 7). Although OPCs, mature oligodendrocytes and myeloid cells were the most abundant, we also annotated fine-grained neurons, astrocytes, lymphocytes and vasculature (Supplementary Note 1). Taken together, our single-nuclei transcriptomic atlas presents a deep, fine-grained cellular census of malignant and TME states in GB.

Next, we examined the spatial organization of GB cell states. To resolve fine GB states in Visium ST data, we mapped malignant and TME clusters from each patient’s snRNA-seq profile to their matched Visium data using cell2location16 (Fig. 2a). Whereas integrating paired snRNA-seq and ST accounted for inter-tumour heterogeneity, it also enabled us to link GB spatial organization to malignant cell trajectories, subclonal organization and TME signalling that we subsequently inferred from snRNA-seq.

a, Workflow for identification of GB spatial TMs that recur across tumours. b, Distinct cellular compositions of recurrent GB TMs. The heatmap depicts the proportion of cell state abundance associated with a given tumour-specific NMF factor. Factors (columns) are ordered by their corresponding spatial microenvironment clusters (top colour bar). The most frequently observed cell states for each microenvironment are shown per row, in which black and blue text represents TME and malignant cells, respectively. c, TM abundances for several Visium ST sections showing key microenvironment distribution patterns in an intratumoural context (AT15) and across different tumours. d, Network diagram illustrating spatial proximity between recurrent TMs. Edge width and colour represent the mean pairwise Euclidean distance between microenvironment spots. e, Xenium sections depicting spatial maps of main cell states in tumour AT10.

GB cell states showed striking segregation across all tumours. In particular, gliosis and hypoxia cell states segregated from dev-like states (Extended Data Fig. 2), consistent with previous surveys10,15. GB states also showed regional heterogeneity across tumour sampling sites (Extended Data Fig. 2 and Supplementary Fig. 8c). We also observed concordant spatial mapping results between cell2location and alternative computational methods, especially for highly abundant GB cell states (Methods and Supplementary Fig. 10a–c).

We then asked whether GBs have a conserved spatial architecture. To determine whether malignant and TME cells assemble into stereotyped tissue microenvironments (TMs), we first identified spatially colocalized cell states (that is, microenvironments) per tumour by means of non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) of cell2location results16 (Fig. 2a and Methods). This resulted in 192 factors across our cohort (Supplementary Table 7 and Supplementary Fig. 11a), which we then clustered by their cell state similarity to identify 16 TMs that recurrently appear across tumours (Fig. 2b).

We annotated the recurrent GB TMs on the basis of their cellular composition and anatomical location (Fig. 2b,c and Supplementary Note 2). ‘Tumour’ TMs represented malignant, immune and vasculature states in the tumour core, whereas ‘infiltrated’ TMs spanned non-malignant neurons and glia in the surrounding infiltrated regions (Fig. 2b,c). Most tumour TMs were defined by their distinct GB cell state composition and appeared across many tumours (Extended Data Fig. 3). Core malignant TMs such as Dev-like (OPC), Dev-like (AC), Proliferative, Gliosis transition, Gliosis and Hypoxic 1 were detected in more than 50% of tumours, whereas others such as Dev-like (Neuron) and Hypoxic 2 were rare. Crucially, 8 out of 12 tumours (for example, AT3, AT10) showed nearly the full complement of core TMs (Extended Data Fig. 3a), suggesting these features are fundamental to GB organization. Finally, we recapitulated these TMs with cell2location alternatives on our GB atlas and on public GB Visium ST datasets10,15 (Methods and Supplementary Fig. 12).

Previous ST studies have mapped hypoxic ‘mesenchymal’-like states at the necrotic core and dev-like states at the infiltrating edge of tumours10,15. Correlating GB TMs with tumour anatomy showed Dev-like TMs occurred in the cellular tumour compartment bordering the infiltrating tumour and leading edge. By contrast, Gliosis and Hypoxia TMs were localized further from the infiltrating regions, forming layered zones around perinecrotic and necrotic areas (Fig. 2c, Extended Data Fig. 3a and Supplementary Note 2).

To quantify their precise spatial arrangement, we calculated the pairwise spatial proximities of GB TMs across all tumours (n = 97 Visium sections) into a network graph (Methods). This showed that GB TMs are ordered along a main anatomical axis between the infiltrating tumour edge and the necrotic tumour core (Fig. 2d). Dev-like (OPC) was found closest to infiltrated white matter. Dev-like (AC) spatially overlapped with the Dev-like (OPC), yet extended deeper into the tumour towards successive layers of Gliosis transition, Gliosis and Hypoxia (Fig. 2d). Dev-like (Neuron) was similarly positioned near the infiltrated regions when present (Fig. 2c). In tumour AT15 that we profiled in whole, these gradual transitions from dev-like TMs to gliosis and hypoxia were observed across each sampling site (Supplementary Fig. 13a,b).

We validated these observations with orthogonal 315-plex Xenium ST data (n = 17 sections from 8 tumours) annotated at the single-cell level by means of snRNA-seq integration (Methods). This validated malignant cell state zonation, in which dev-like states bordered infiltrated regions marked by neurons, contrasting with the gliosis and hypoxia states situated further around necrosis (Fig. 2e and Supplementary Fig. 13c). Profiling centimetre-scale tumour sections revealed this pattern at each sampling site (Fig. 2e), indicating stereotyped spatial organization throughout each tumour. Xenium also enabled us to validate the accuracy of cell2location predictions on GB data (Methods and Supplementary Fig. 14).

GB TMs also reflected TME organization. ‘Vasculature’ captured pericytes, VLMCs and endothelial cells, anatomically correlated with microvascular proliferation and hyperplastic blood vessels, and was found in close proximity to Dev-like (AC) and (OPC), Gliosis transition and Proliferative malignant TMs (Fig. 2b,d and Extended Data Fig. 3a). Two ‘Immune’ TMs captured distinct myeloid cell compartments (last section). Among infiltrated regions, ‘White matter’ was found in close proximity to tumour leading edge (Fig. 2c,d), consistent with being a main GB invasion route17,18,19.

Taken together, we reveal stereotyped stepwise spatial transitions of malignant cells from dev-like to gliosis and hypoxia states in GB.

We proposed that the stereotyped spatial transitions of GB states relates to their cellular trajectories. Specifically, we proposed that as GB tumours expand at their leading edge into normal brain tissue, the dev-like malignant cells progressively transition towards gliosis and hypoxia states. To test this, we first examined putative malignant trajectories related to gliosis and hypoxia.

In the snRNA-seq data, we observed an expression gradient of astrocyte, injury response and hypoxia-related genes through AC-gliosis-hypoxia states (Fig. 3a). The AC-prog-like states showed the highest levels of developmental and homeostatic astrocyte gene expression (EGFR, SLC1A3, AQP4, ALDH1L1). These were downregulated in AC-gliosis-like cells and replaced by a transcriptomic program resembling astrogliosis, including genes from the integrin–N-cadherin pathway (ITGAV, ITGB1, CDH2) associated with glial scar formation20. This program expanded in gliosis-like cells to genes associated with JAK–STAT signalling (JAK2, STAT3, SMARC4), wound healing (ANXA2, ANXA5, YAP1, F1, AKAP12), cytokine production (IFI16, IL6R, IL1R1) and coagulation (SERPINE1), as well as angiogenesis and hypoxia (VEGFA)21,22,23. This trajectory terminated in hypoxia (HILPDA, BNIP3L, VEGFA) and stress-response gene expression (JUN, FOS, HSPA1B) (Fig. 3a and Extended Data Fig. 4a). Transcriptome-wide pseudotime analysis produced consistent results (Methods and Supplementary Fig. 15).

a, Transcriptional continuum across AC-gliosis-hypoxia GB cell states. Left, marker gene expression across states in snRNA-seq, showing relative z-score normalized gene expression (colour) and proportion of cells per state expressing the gene (size). Centre, pathway enrichment across states in snRNA-seq, showing the z-score normalized enrichment score (colour) and the −log[P] of each comparison (size). Right, spatial correlation of cell states with anatomical features in Visium ST data, showing the Pearson’s correlation coefficient (r) (colour) and relative abundance of a cell state within feature-annotated Visium spots (size). b, Spatial zonation of main AC-gliosis-hypoxia GB states and marker gene expression in ST data and immunohistochemistry validation. Left, cell state abundance (top panel, colour) and gene expression (bottom panel, colour) in Visium ST data. Middle, cell states (top and bottom panel, multi-colour maps) and marker genes (bottom panels, colour) in Xenium ST data. Right, antibody staining showing distinct zonation of AKAP12 (gliosis-hypoxia) and HILPDA (hypoxia) (n = 3 tumours independently imaged). c, Network diagram summarizing the spatial proximity of relevant cell states in Visium data, with coloured banners indicating the primary spatial microenvironment of each cell state, and boxes indicating the associated histological features. d, Schematic summarizing the AC-gliosis transcriptional gradient in a histological context, including relevant functional axes. prog., progenitor. Scale bars, 1 mm.

Whereas they were previously thought to resemble mesenchymal cells2, we observed negligible and non-specific expression of key epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition regulators (for example, SNAI1/2, TWIST1/2, ZEB1/2) in gliosis-hypoxia states24,25 (Extended Data Fig. 4a). Hence, our nomenclature places these states in the more specific biological context of glial injury response and hypoxia, putatively stemming from developmental astrocyte-like malignant cells.

The molecular trajectory was correspondingly patterned in space, manifesting as concentric segregation of AC-gliosis-hypoxia states in ST data (Fig. 3b,c and Extended Data Fig. 4c). AC-prog-like cells resided in the non-necrotic cellular tumour in the Dev-like (AC) microenvironment. AC-gliosis-like and gliosis-like cells formed Gliosis transition and Gliosis microenvironments, respectively, that spatially intermixed to varying degrees. In tumours such as AT10, AC-gliosis-like was located at the margin of the cellular tumour and gradually transitioned into gliosis-like within the perinecrotic zone. Hypoxic cells were located either within or adjacent to the tumour necrotic core. The marker genes of these states showed consistent zonated expression with ST and immunohistochemistry (Fig. 3b and Extended Data Fig. 4b).

Taken together, we identify putative GB cellular transitions from developmental astrocyte-like to gliosis then hypoxia states, unfolding across an anatomical axis from tumour expansion towards hypoxia and necrosis (Fig. 3d).

To explore GB cellular transitions, we then asked whether dev-like and gliosis-hypoxic states could emerge within the same tumour subclones (that is, genetically related malignant sublineages). Initially, we performed copy number aberration (CNA) inference to our multiome data, jointly calling clones from tumour snRNA-seq and snATAC-seq profiles (Fig. 4a and Supplementary Note 3). Distinguished by chr. 7 and chr. 10 CNs, most tumour subclones contained both dev-like and gliosis-hypoxic cells (Fig. 4b and Supplementary Fig. 16b,c), with the minority states making up an average of 15% (ranging from 3% to 49%) of each clone. Whereas subclones tended to show similar GB state compositions, three tumours contained individual subclones with divergent states. For example, tumour AT10 clone 0 was marked by chr. 17p loss and chr. 17q gain and was preferentially enriched for NPC-neuronal-like states, whereas AT10 clone 1 was enriched for AC-gliosis-hypoxia (Fig. 4b).

a, Multiome CNA-calling workflow. The joint clonal annotation in tumour AT10 is illustrated by heatmaps from paired snRNA-seq (top) and snATAC-seq (bottom) data showing putative copy gain (red) and copy loss (blue). The harmonized clone annotations are indicated by the left sidebar. Insets highlight a main lineage-defining CN changes to chr. 17. b, Bar plots depicting cell state distributions across clones (right) and clone distribution across tumour sampling sites (left) in CNA-inferred clones. c, LCM-WGS-based spatial clone mapping workflow. The H&E images show a tumour ROI before and after LCM, marked by an asterisk. d, LCM genotypes in the snRNA-seq data as identified by alleleIntegrator. Left, phylogeny illustrating lineage-defining mutations. Right, B-allele frequency plot showing the LCM-based SNP-phasing applied to genotype the single nucleus data for two putative clones. e, Spatially intermixed GB subclones in LCM-WGS data. Bar plot summarizes pyclone-VI clone distributions for each LCM ROI and clonal cluster. f, SpaceTree workflow for joint spatial mapping of cell states and tumour subclones by means of integration of ST and snRNA-seq data. g, GB subclones spatially overlap with both dev-like and gliosis-hypoxia cell states. SpaceTree-derived cell state (top) and clonal (bottom) maps in tumour AT15 are shown. The bar plots summarize the distribution of cell states across spots in which a given clone is the most abundant. h, Clonal entropy of Visium spots based on SpaceTree mapping binned across tumour purity fractions. High entropy (that is, clonal intermixing) is observed in tissue regions with high tumour purity. Boxplots show median, interquartile range (IQR) and 1.5× IQR whiskers (n = 188,933 spots total across n = 97 Visium sections). i, GB clonal organization summary diagram. Scale bars, 100 µm.

To identify CNAs and subclones at the DNA level, we performed WGS on 100–200 × 100–200-μm sized tissue regions of interest (ROIs) by means of laser capture microdissection (LCM)26 (Fig. 4c). We profiled several ROIs across two sampling sites of two tumours (AT3, AT10), generating 61 high-quality WGS profiles (Supplementary Fig. 17). Notably, one ROI from AT10 showed a CN loss in chr. 17p and gain chr. 17q, validating our multiome CN calls. We then defined tumour subclones in multiome data on the basis of the CN events validated by means of LCM-WGS27 (Extended Data Fig. 5a). In AT10, this validated chr. 7 gain and chr. 10 loss in malignant cells and distinguished two subclones based on chr. 17 alterations (Fig. 4d). Both subclones contained a mixture of dev-like and gliosis-hypoxia cells, with clone L0 enriched for NPC-neuronal-like cells and marked by chr. 17 CNs (Extended Data Fig. 5b,c), mirroring our multiome findings. Hence, paired multi-omic evidence demonstrates shared clonal origins of dev-like and gliosis-hypoxia cell states.

Next, we examined spatial organization of GB subclones and whether each subclone spans dev-like to gliosis-hypoxia TMs. In the multiome data, we detected many subclones within each centimetre-scale tumour sampling site (Fig. 4b and Supplementary Fig. 18a). Different sampling sites showed largely consistent clonal composition, with exceptions including AT10, in which the chr. 17-altered clone 0 is predominantly located in one site (Fig. 4b). These data indicate coarse spatial intermixing of GB clones, as shown in refs. 5,7.

To investigate finer-scale clonal organization, we examined our LCM-WGS data (roughly 100 × 100 µm resolution). Considering GB clonal intermixing and that our LCM cuts span many cells, we used PyClone-VI28 to infer clonal population structure of LCM ROIs on the basis of single nucleotide variant (SNV) allele frequencies (Fig. 4c). Focusing on AT3, our most comprehensively profiled tumour, we identified 14 SNV clusters (that is, putative subclones) across 35 ROIs (Supplementary Fig. 18c). Individual SNV clusters were present across several LCM ROIs and individual ROIs contained several SNV clusters, indicating clonal intermixing at fine spatial resolution (Fig. 4e).

Clustering ROIs on the basis of their subclonal composition revealed broad spatial clonal domains spanning several millimetres (Fig. 4e and Extended Data Fig. 5g). Broad spatial gradients of intermixed subclones demarcated these domains (Supplementary Note 4). Different tumour sampling sites showed more extensive clonal differences than suggested by multiome CNA inference (Extended Data Fig. 5g), probably owing to the better sensitivity of SNV-based clone calling. Inferring the AT3 phylogeny (Methods), we observed a high degree of spatial intermixture between ancestral (that is, 12), mid-timed (that is, 9) and late (that is, 4) SNV clusters (Fig. 4d,e and Supplementary Figs. 18c and 19).

Individual clones and clonal domains spanned diverse GB cell states and TMs resolved on the adjacent Visium sections (Supplementary Fig. 18c). As our LCM-WGS dataset was limited to two tumours, we then surveyed clonal organization across our Visium dataset. To resolve GB subclones intermixed within Visium spots, we developed the SpaceTree computational framework that leverages scRNA-seq to jointly deconvolve tumour subclones and cell states in ST data (Fig. 4f). SpaceTree integrates reference scRNA-seq and query ST datasets by means of a multi-task graph neural network architecture coupled with label propagation, enabling joint spatial mapping of clones and cell states annotated in scRNA-seq (Supplementary Fig. 20a and Supplementary Computational Note).

We benchmarked SpaceTree on ST data simulated from our GB snRNA-seq profiles, finding that it offers spatial clone deconvolution accuracy near alternative tools at notably reduced computational cost (Supplementary Computational Note). We then applied SpaceTree to integrate our GB snRNA-seq and Visium ST data per tumour site, leveraging our cell annotation and multiome clone calls. As expected, SpaceTree distinguished tumour versus normal and/or infiltrated regions on the basis of the spatial mapping of malignant versus diploid and/or TME clones, respectively (Extended Data Fig. 5h,j and Supplementary Note 4).

SpaceTree revealed widespread spatial intermixing of subclones across all tumours (Fig. 4g and Supplementary Fig. 20b), quantified as high clonal entropy in Visium spots dominated by malignant cells and TMs (Fig. 4h and Supplementary Note 4). SpaceTree also resolved broad spatial subclonal domains that overlapped with diverse malignant cell states (Extended Data Fig. 5i and Supplementary Fig. 20c,e). For example, AT15 subclones 0, 3 and 4 each overlapped with both dev-like and gliosis-hypoxia cell states (Fig. 4g). Yet, we also observed regional clonal enrichment, such as clone 3 contributing more heavily to gliosis-hypoxia (Fig. 4g) and the AT10 clone 0 marked by chr. 17 CNs enriched in tissue areas with NPC-neuronal-like cells (Extended Data Fig. 5i). Finally, we observed concordant spatial clonal mapping between SpaceTree and LCM-WGS (Extended Data Fig. 5g and Supplementary Note 4).

In summary, we present a new framework for GB subclonal spatial architecture (Fig. 4i), in which individual subclones finely spatially intermix and organize into broad clonal domains cutting across GB TMs.

Given their shared clonal origins in single-cell and spatial data, we proposed that dev-like cells continuously transition into gliosis and hypoxia states during the rapid expansion of GBs, which double in size every 50 days (ref. 29), and that our ‘snapshot’ snRNA-seq profiling can capture the different stages of such transitions. To infer cellular trajectories from snRNA-seq, we used cell2fate, a probabilistic RNA velocity model30 (Extended Data Fig. 6a).

We applied cell2fate to the snRNA-seq profiles of individual tumour subclones, avoiding confounding genetic differences across clones and tumours, and reconstructed robust trajectories from 23 out of 58 subclones (Extended Data Fig. 6b,c and Supplementary Note 5). Most of these subclones (18 out of 23, more than 78%) showed temporal transitions from dev-like to AC-gliosis-hypoxia and the rest were dominated by an individual state and often showed low transition scores (less than 0.2; 6 out of 7, 86%) (Fig. 5a and Extended Data Figs. 6b–e and 7a).

a, Cell2fate analysis resolving a trajectory from dev-like to AC-gliosis-hypoxia states across GB subclones and tumours. Top panel, streamgraph plots show cell state occurrence across inferred trajectory time across 23 subclones (rows). Clones clustered on the basis of the ranked temporal order of coarse-grained cell states. Second panel, bar plot depicting temporal cell state abundance in clone AT10_1. Third panel, boxplot showing the latent time distribution of each cell class for all diverse clones (Shannon entropy of cell states more than 0.5). Bottom panel, line plot showing the consistent differences in latent time between dev-like and AC-gliosis-hypoxia cell states within each clone. Lines coloured by Shannon entropy. Difference in latent time evaluated using a one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test. b, Comparison between dev-like and AC-gliosis-hypoxia cell state abundances and clone population distributions in paired Visium ST and LCM-WGS data. Top, phylogenetic relationships inferred using PairTree with putative timing indicated by blue (early) and orange (late). Bottom, Pearson correlation coefficients and two-tailed P values with 95% confidence intervals calculated between PairTree-inferred clone distributions and the fraction of total cell state abundances of a given cell state across all Visium spots matching LCM ROIs. c, GBO engraftment experimental workflow. d, Cell state composition of engrafted E25 and E30 GFP+ cells across time. D0 composition is inferred from scRNA-seq of pre-engrafted cell lines. e, Spatial organization of background GBO cells (left) and the GFP+ engrafted E25 cells (right) at D14. Top, segmented cells coloured by cell state identity (see d for legend). Inset, radial zonation across the periphery-to-core axis. Middle, boxplots summarizing minimum–maximum-normalized cellular distances to the GBO periphery across pooled timepoints of E25-engrafted GBOs. Boxplots show median, IQR and 1.5× IQR whiskers (n = 3 GBOs, n = 8 sections per GBO). Bottom, normalized expression of cell state marker genes in E25-engrafted GBOs computed across the normalized distance to the GBO periphery. f, Summary diagram of the GB spatiotemporal cancer cell trajectory. Scale bars, 200 μm. Illustration in c created in BioRender; Lee, J. https://biorender.com/etd6tah (2026).

We observed this trajectory across six out of the nine tumours (for example, AT4, AT10, AT15), in which both NPC-neuronal-like (AT15_0) or OPC-NPC-like (AT6_0) states led to AC-gliosis-hypoxia (Fig. 5a). GBs of all presumed subtypes showed this transition, including the NPC-OPC-like enriched ‘proneural’ (for example, AT5), the NPC-neuronal-like enriched ‘neural’ (that is, AT15) and the AC-gliosis-hypoxia enriched ‘classical-mesenchymal’ (for example, AT6) tumours (Fig. 5a). Within each tumour, many subclones converged on this trajectory (for example, chr. 17 CN+/− clones in AT10). Hence, this trajectory dominates GBs across tumour subtypes and genetically distinct subclones.

Next, we examined whether this cellular trajectory is molecularly conserved across GB, leveraging temporal gene expression modules (that is, RNA velocity modules) identified by cell2fate30 (Supplementary Note 5). We identified 12 meta-modules representing recurrent temporal transcriptional programs across subclones and tumours (Extended Data Fig. 8a). Dev-like modules occurred early in the trajectory, were enriched in dev-like states and shared their marker genes (for example, MBP, MYT1L). By contrast, AC-gliosis-hypoxia modules occurred late and were enriched in AC-gliosis-hypoxia states with respective marker gene expression (for example, GFAP, SERPINE1, HILPDA). Consistently, mapped in Visium ST data, these modules showed spatial transitions akin to those from dev-like to gliosis-hypoxia cell states (Extended Data Fig. 8b). Furthermore, survival analysis identified worse outcomes for patients enriched for late gliosis-hypoxia modules (Supplementary Note 5 and Supplementary Fig. 22), consistent with poor ‘mesenchymal-like’ GB prognosis1,31. Finally, these modules also nominated new candidate regulators and effectors of GB cellular trajectories (Supplementary Note 5). Hence, this trajectory is spatially patterned and molecularly conserved across GBs.

To orthogonally validate the GB trajectory, we initially used somatic mutations in our most extensive LCM-WGS dataset (tumour AT3) to reconstruct GB clonal phylogenies. This delivered a SNV-based hierarchy of clones (Fig. 5b and Methods), more finely resolving clonal architecture than CNA inference, which we then correlated with GB cell states mapped in adjacent Visium ST sections. We focused on the most ancestral and the most frequently observed late SNV clusters, 0 and 4, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 18c). The abundance of the ancestral SNV cluster 0 was positively correlated with NPC-OPC-like cell states and negatively correlated with AC-gliosis-hypoxia, whereas the late SNV cluster 4 showed the opposite pattern (Fig. 5b). These data are consistent with a GB trajectory along which AC-gliosis-hypoxia cell states are derived from NPC-OPC-like cells.

To experimentally validate the GB trajectory, we engrafted patient-derived GB cell lines into patient-derived tumour organoids and traced their population-level cellular trajectories over time in situ (Fig. 5c and Supplementary Note 6). First, we derived GB organoids (GBOs) from a primary IDH-wt tumour32. Using 5,101-plex Xenium ST (Methods), we observed that GBOs recapitulate the spatial transitions of GB cell states, in which NPC-OPC-like states were located most peripherally, AC-progenitor-like states were positioned relatively deeper and Gliosis-like states formed an inner ring around the hypoxic core (Fig. 5e and Extended Data Fig. 9d). Second, to trace the cellular trajectories arising from dev-like GB cells, we characterized two dev-like patient lines33, E25 and E30, labelled them with green fluorescent protein (GFP) reporters and engrafted them into GBOs (Methods). At pre-engraftment (day 0, D0), scRNA-seq showed that E25 overwhelmingly consisted of dev-like states (89.2% OPC/NPC-OPC-like), whereas E30 was a mix of dev-like (25.7%) and AC-gliosis-like cells (48.1%) (Fig. 5d).

We then separately engrafted E25 and E30 GFP+ cells into 3-week old GBOs and used 5,101-plex Xenium ST to profile their spatiotemporal trajectories until D28 (Fig. 5c, Extended Data Fig. 9 and Supplementary Note 6). After GBO engraftment, the dev-like E25 line gave rise to AC-gliosis-hypoxia cells (Fig. 5d,e). At D7 and D14, engrafted cells showed expected spatial patterns, in which OPC-NPC-like and AC-prog-like GFP+ cells were located most peripherally, the Gliosis-like GFP+ cells were positioned deeper and the hypoxic GFP+ cells were at the GBO core (Fig. 5e, right panel, and Supplementary Fig. 24a). Consistently, in the E30 engrafts, dev-like cells reduced and AC-gliosis-hypoxia states accumulated over time (Fig. 5d and Extended Data Fig. 9e), manifesting fine-grained cellular transitions akin to patient tumours (Supplementary Note 6).

Taken together, we identify and validate a spatially patterned and molecularly conserved malignant cell trajectory across GBs. Combined with our fine-grained mapping of AC-gliosis-hypoxia trajectories (Fig. 3), these data indicate stepwise transitions of malignant cells from dev-like towards gliosis and hypoxia states throughout tumour expansion (Fig. 5f).

Finally, we investigated whether the GB TME is specialized to accommodate the GB malignant cell trajectory. We focused on myeloid cells, given their prevalence (Supplementary Table 3) and that macrophage-derived signals can alter GB malignant cell states9. We annotated myeloid subclusters in our snRNA-seq atlas by expression of canonical markers, MSigDB gene sets and glioma myeloid programs34.

We classified 11 myeloid subtypes, most being tumour-associated macrophages (TAMs), into 3 main classes (Extended Data Fig. 10a and Supplementary Note 7): (1) resident and pro-inflammatory myeloid cells (P2RY12, CX3CR1) spanning microglia and anti-tumour TAMs, (2) infiltrating and anti-inflammatory myeloid cells (CD163, STAB1, CD14) including monocytes and TAMs showing immunosuppressive and protumour signatures and (3) stress-response and angiogenic TAMs expressing hypoxia and angiogenesis (VEGFA, VCAN) and ‘lipid-laden’ macrophage (GPNMB, PLIN2) markers.

To precisely relate these myeloid cell states to GB states, we examined their distribution across GB TMs and observed spatially distinct myeloid compartments (Extended Data Fig. 10a,b and Supplementary Note 7). Resident and pro-inflammatory populations were enriched in the ‘Immune (resident)’ TM overlapping with dev-like GB cells (for example, OPC-like). Infiltrating and anti-inflammatory populations formed the distinct ‘Immune (infiltrated)’ TM in closer proximity to AC-like and Gliosis-transition states. Stress-response and angiogenic TAMs were highly enriched in the ‘Gliosis’ and ‘Hypoxia’ TMs.

These observations indicate distinct myeloid microenvironments for dev-like and gliosis-hypoxia GB cell states. To determine whether these malignant states are exposed to distinct myeloid signals, we performed cell–cell communication (CCC) analysis in snRNA-seq data among spatially colocalized TME and malignant states (Extended Data Fig. 10c and Supplementary Note 7). This analysis identified distinct myeloid signalling environments across the GB cellular trajectory (Extended Data Fig. 10d,e). In dev-like TMs, myeloid ligands linked to protumour and anti-tumour functions, such as TRAIL (TNFSF10), progranulin (GRN) and galectin 9 (LGALS9), putatively signalled to dev-like states. In gliosis-hypoxia TMs, distinct myeloid ligands linked to wound healing, hypoxia and angiogenesis, such VEGFA, versican (VCAN) and annexin 1 (ANXA1) putatively targeted gliosis and hypoxic cancer cells (Supplementary Note 7).

Taken together, the myeloid TME is regionalized across the GB malignant cell trajectory and exposes malignant cells to distinct signals (Supplementary Fig. 28).

GB heterogeneity and plasticity have undermined efforts to pinpoint the cellular trajectories of cancer cells and develop targeted therapies. Here we applied a holistic multimodal mapping approach to jointly characterize the genetic, cellular and tissue architecture of GB tumours. We describe remarkable intra-tumour heterogeneity and spatial organization of GBs, extending previous surveys. Yet, we distinctly link GB heterogeneity and tissue architecture to a spatiotemporally patterned cancer cell trajectory from dev-like towards glial injury response and hypoxia states. This trajectory is molecularly conserved across presumed GB tumour subtypes and subclonal lineages within each tumour, and is recapitulated in GBOs ex vivo. Furthermore, it is coupled to regionalized myeloid TME signalling. Hence, this trajectory represents a fundamental organizational principle of GB tumours unifying their heterogeneity.

Our multimodal atlas facilitated the biological reinterpretation of GB cancer cell states. Notably, we found that the previously reported mesenchymal cell state1,2 was in fact a malignant cell gliosis and hypoxia response. Wound healing-like states and hypoxia are present across many cancers including pancreatic35 and colon36 cancer, suggesting dev-like cancer cells transitioning into such states may be conserved37. Beyond hypoxia, whether other cell and tissue cues push dev-like cancer states into gliosis remains to be identified.

The spatiotemporal trajectory of cancer cells challenges the stratification of GB tumours into distinct subtypes. The regional heterogeneity within each tumour suggests that GB subtypes, commonly classified from single biopsies, rather represent region-specific cancer cell states and TMs. The temporal nature of the GB trajectory may pose another challenge. Tumours enriched for dev-like or gliosis-hypoxia states may represent early or advanced stages of GB, respectively, possibly accounting for the worse survival outcomes of mesenchymal GBs1.

Genetic alterations can promote distinct cancer cell states across GBs2. Whereas the GB trajectory is shared across the tumour genetic hierarchy, our results also raise the possibility that GB cell states can be modulated within genetically distinct subclones. Exemplified here by the association of chr. 17 CN events with neuronal-like cancer cell states, previously documented in medulloblastomas38,39, functional studies are needed to determine whether genetic alterations can expand intra-tumour heterogeneity.

We identify multi-scale spatial architecture of GB cancer cell subclones. Whereas GB subclones parcellate tumours into broad spatial domains, we observe their intimate spatial intermixture within each domain. Contrasting with the spatial segregation of clones in breast40 and prostate41 cancer, this pattern may reflect the lack of physical barriers in the brain, such as ductal structures in the breast40, that can restrict clonal outgrowth, as well as the migratory nature of GB cancer cells.

In a companion study, we leveraged the joint transcriptomic and epigenetic data generated here to define and perturb gene regulatory networks controlling GB plasticity12. Beyond identifying master regulators of GB states, this orthogonal approach suggested hierarchical transitions across GB cancer states and recapitulated the GB trajectory identified here.

Our study has several limitations. First, although we trace population-level cellular trajectories in organoids, we do not provide single cancer cell-resolution lineage tracing42. Second, whereas we examine the dominant cellular trajectories of cancer cells in primary GB, we do not interrogate their plasticity potential. Specifically, previous studies and ours2,6 do not resolve whether GB cancer cells can revert from gliosis and hypoxia into dev-like states. Yet, our companion study predicts limited cell state transitions of gliosis-hypoxia cells on the basis of gene regulatory networks12, raising the possibility of limited cancer cell plasticity in GB beyond the trajectory illustrated here.

The significant intratumoural heterogeneity of GB underscores the challenges to therapeutic intervention. Our findings propose targeting the spatiotemporal trajectory of cancer cells and destabilizing the myeloid TME associated with this trajectory, two conserved features of GB tumours identified here, as potential avenues for exploration.

Patients with suspected GB were identified pre-operatively and consented for entry into the study. Surgery was performed at Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust. Written and informed consent was obtained in accordance with the guidelines in The Declaration of Helsinki 2000. Ethical approval for the use of these tissues was obtained from the Cambridge Local Research Ethics Committee (REC 18/EE/0172). All patients underwent 5-aminolevulinic acid (5-ALA) guided tumour resection as per local protocols. During tumour debulking, regions of high fluorescence were identified, their spatial location recorded and the tissue samples were collected for this study. Matched whole blood was taken during surgery for germline characterization. The clinical characteristics of the patient cohort and samples are detailed in Supplementary Table 1.

Tissue was sampled from several sites of each GB tumour, targeting superior, anterior, posterior and middle regions where possible. Each tissue sample was immediately washed in saline buffer and embedded in optimal cutting temperature (OCT) medium (Scigen OCT Compound, 4586) using a dry ice-cooled bath of isopentane at −75 °C. OCT-embedded samples were sectioned using a cryostat (Leica CX3050S). The fresh-frozen tissue blocks were trimmed until the tissue surface was fully exposed. Two to three 10-µm thick sections were collected to check RNA integrity and another section was processed for haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining to assess tissue morphology. The RNA quality of each sample was evaluated by Tapestation (Tapestation RNA ScreenTape, Agilent) after isolating RNA (Qiagen EZ2 Automated RNA Extraction using EZ2 RNA/micro-RNA Tissue Kit, 959035). Only samples with RNA integrity number values above 7 were used for omic profiling.
